terms.gloss: liberal: holding free views about the state
terms.comment: A modern description in classical words; Morgan–Owens and Traupman give no term. Traupman gives optimātēs for the conservatives of ancient Rome (p. 178), but the optimātēs were the men who worked through the senate and the leading families, and the populārēs those who worked through the people’s assemblies (Cic. Sest. 96, Lewis & Short s.v. optimās): methods and alliances, not programmes. Neither is a modern conservative or liberal party, and the words are best not used for them.

A false friend for the political sense: classically worthy of a free man, gentlemanly, kind, and above all generous (Lewis & Short). In that sense it is the right word; the liberal arts are artēs līberālēs (see culture).

sources: Lewis & Short: liberalis · Lewis & Short: libere · Lewis & Short: sentio · Lewis & Short: optimas · Lewis & Short: popularis
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 38, s.v. liberale.
